items.quote: THE Admonitory Preface OF OSWALD CROLLIE, Physitian
items.note: The text heads itself as one writing, the Admonitory Preface of Oswald Crollie, physician; the heading names Prince Christian Anhaltin as addressee, while OPEN.1 and OPEN.3 address the reader.

items.quote: the Romans extolled Angerona, and the Grecians admired Hapocrotes for their silence
items.note: Opens by naming figures praised for their silence: silence about secrets is set up as the received norm the author is about to depart from.

items.name: ancient Philosophers
items.quote: all the ancient Philosophers, by the example of Actaeon, have strictly forbidden to prophane the Secrets
items.note: A rule given to the ancient Philosophers: the Secrets must not be profaned.

items.quote: rashly to prostitute the Treasures of Nature to unworthy and filthy minded men
items.note: The forbidden thing is giving the Treasures of Nature to unworthy men: the secrets are meant for some readers only.

items.quote: for he communicateth his light, without respect or envy, to the good and bad
items.note: God shares his light with all alike; this is the ground the author gives for sharing.

items.quote: We are bound to immitate him whose Children we ought to be
items.note: Against the rule of silence, the author holds that men must imitate God's open giving.

items.name: Psal. 145.9. Mat. 5. Luke 19. John 1.5.
items.quote: Psal. 145.9. Mat. 5. Luke 19. John 1.5
items.note: Margin note naming scripture places beside the sentence on God shining on all alike.

items.name: Strabe
items.quote: men imitate God, when they do good
items.note: Margin saying given to Strabe beside the duty to imitate God.

items.name: Victor
items.quote: The gifts of God grow, & are improved by communicating
items.note: Margin saying given to Victor: God's gifts grow by being shared.

items.quote: brought back and recovered from the dark Labyrinth and Circumference of toyle and error, to the plain and clear path and Centre of Rest and Truth
items.note: Paired figures (Labyrinth and Circumference against path and Centre) describe a return from error to truth; the plain sense is given only through the figure.

items.quote: any longer to hide as in a Napkin, the Talent committed to me by the Father of Lights, by an impious silence
items.note: The author says he has kept something hidden until now and will no longer do so; keeping it hidden is called impious silence.

items.quote: the Gates of Wisdome ought alwayes to stand open to ingenious men
items.note: Wisdom should stay open, but the sentence names ingenious men as those it stands open to.

items.quote: It is, doubtlesse, a most civil and humane Office, willingly to instruct and guide our erring neighbor
items.note: Teaching the erring neighbour is called a humane duty.

items.quote: I doe here out of the most deep secret of my heart, set before thee two of the most excellent Spagyrik Mysteries
items.what: two of the most excellent Spagyrik Mysteries
items.note: The text announces what it offers as two things: two Spagyrik Mysteries.

items.quote: out of the most deep secret of my heart
items.note: What is offered is said to come from the author's deepest secret: something till now withheld.

items.quote: have all of them been first proved by my own handy experience
items.note: The author states that the preparations of the two Mysteries were all tried first by his own hand.

items.quote: which neither by report nor ancient Records, I could yet understand that they have together and at once been published unto this very day
items.note: He claims the two have not before been published together.

items.quote: Some of these have beene prepared by others for the Emperor Rudolph to whom I voluntarily imparted them
items.note: Margin note: some of these were imparted by the author to Emperor Rudolph and prepared by others for him.

items.quote: much lesse to fill up a huge Volume with the copies of large Receipts
items.note: He refuses to fill the book with many receipts, though he says he has many.

items.quote: The greatest Receipts the greatest Deceits for the most part
items.note: Margin note: the largest receipts are mostly deceits.

items.quote: I would first take my eyes in my hand, as I may so say, and by the help of Vulcan search and diligently examine the chief and choycest things
items.note: The text flags its own figure (as I may so say) and names Vulcan as the helper of examination; OPEN.5 speaks of the Art of Fire and the triall of fire, which suggests (my inference) that Vulcan here stands for fire.

items.quote: before I would commend them to publick use and profit
items.note: The work described: examining the chosen things by Vulcan before releasing them for public use.

items.quote: I have obtained from men of greatest learning and experience in Chymistry, partly by intreaty, partly by purchase and permutation
items.note: He says much of what he offers came from others, by asking, buying and exchange, over almost twenty years of travel.

items.name: Plin in Epist. ad Vesp.
items.quote: It is a Civil thing, and full of ingenious modesty, to acknowledge by whom we gained any thing
items.note: Margin saying given to Pliny: acknowledge from whom one learned; stands beside the account of his sources.

items.quote: the Children of knowledge, those searchers out and lovers of Truth
items.note: The text glosses Children of knowledge as searchers out and lovers of Truth.

items.quote: not fallacious opinions (as hitherto in such a deale of Legerdemain they have complained of) but the truth it self so long desired
items.note: He sets what he gives (truth found by experiment) against earlier writing called Legerdemain.

items.quote: So that many things after the revolution of the Platonick year have been returned gratis, and with usury to their owners, whole and entire, and far more compleat
items.note: A figure: what he got from others in poor state is returned to them complete and improved; the Platonick year is not explained in the lines given.

items.quote: those things which they bragged of as great secrets, seemed to me either common, or so faulty and defective
items.note: Many so-called great secrets of others he found common or defective.

items.quote: the imperfection of their many descriptions, was to be made up by me, being all reduced into one onely, and that same first proved by my own Chymicall triall
items.note: His method: many defective descriptions are combined into a single one, then tried by his own chymical trial.

items.name: common Chymicall custome
items.quote: according to that common Chymicall custome, Give something, and take something
items.note: A saying given to chymists' common custom of exchange.

items.quote: in our Conference they got an Egg for a Nut, which when I had crackt with long and fruitlesse paines, I found at last nothing but a worm-eaten kernel
items.note: Figure of a bad exchange: he gave much and received little of worth.

items.name: Poets
items.quote: Vulcan, which the Poets commend as the most true Inventer and Teacher of Arts Mysteries
items.note: The Poets are said to praise Nature's Vulcan as inventor and teacher of the Art's mysteries.

items.quote: who have written in our time of the more secret Spagyrical preparations from other mens relation & not their own handy experience
items.note: He blames recent writers who wrote from hearsay, not their own hand, for students' lost cost and labour.

items.quote: by the help of Pyrotechnye, or the Art of Fire and Chymistry
items.note: The text glosses Pyrotechnye as the Art of Fire and Chymistry.

items.quote: as many things are spoken of which are never done, so many things fall out between the Theory and the Practice
items.note: Theory and practice part ways; much is said that is never done.

items.quote: in this study no man is further to be believed, then as every one findeth by his own proper experience
items.note: Only one's own experience is to be believed in this study.

items.quote: the due approved triall of fire, which discerneth and separateth that which is false, from that which is true
items.note: Trial by fire is the test that separates false from true.

items.quote: Learn by other mens warnings to beware
items.note: Margin note: take warning from others' losses.

items.name: Aeschylus
items.quote: Not he that knowes many things, but he that knowes those things that are most profitable, is to be accounted a wise man
items.note: Saying given to Aeschylus, used to justify offering few things.

items.name: Damascen
items.quote: Let thy Medicines be few, whose vertue and operations thou hast often tryed
items.note: Saying given to Damascen: few medicines, often tried.

items.quote: there doth not lye hid any more choyce and efficacious, then these chief secrets of the more hidden Medicines here offered
items.note: He claims nothing in nature is more effective than the hidden medicines offered here, with one exception.

items.quote: except only that universall and most famous Medicine which the most ancient wise Philosophers had from the beginning of the world
items.what: that universall and most famous Medicine
items.note: One thing is set apart above his medicines: the universal Medicine of the ancient wise Philosophers.

items.quote: have extoll'd it as a miracle to their just and lawfull Heirs
items.note: The universal Medicine was praised to lawful heirs only: knowledge meant for some.

items.name: Anaxagoras
items.quote: See Anaxagoras in his Book
items.note: Margin note naming Anaxagoras beside the claim that nothing in nature lies hid more efficacious; the book title is a gap.

items.quote: for that which is good is not alway to be found in that which is great, but that which is great in that which is good
items.note: Goodness over size: supports offering few things.

items.quote: shall sincerely and as he ought come to the inner rooms of Nature by a holy assiduitie of preparations, joining thereto a diligent contemplation of naturall causes
items.note: Figure of entering nature's inner rooms; the way named is preparation joined with contemplation of natural causes.

items.quote: if the grace of the most high favour be infused into him
items.note: Success in bringing forth greater things is made conditional on divine grace.

items.quote: bring forth far greater things out of this open bosome of Nature
items.note: Nature is called an open bosom: what is hidden is said to be reachable by work.

items.quote: The fruit and great gaine will over and above recompeuce the labour & paines of the Artist
items.note: Margin note: the gain repays the Artist's labour.

items.quote: I have proved but some of those virtues and operations which are assigned to every one in order
items.note: Here he has tried only some of the virtues and operations; OPEN.3 says the preparations were all proved by his own hand. The two may speak of different things (preparations against virtues).

items.quote: as I have set down and shewed their preparations in the work it self
items.note: Points to the work that follows, where the preparations are set down.

items.quote: the Spagyriks, or those who know how to discern between true and false
items.note: The text glosses Spagyriks as those who can tell true from false.

items.quote: I mean the Sons of Art, who know the tearms and bounds thereof
items.note: Sons of Art are those who know the Art's terms and bounds.

items.quote: who can even by a glance and sight only make a good construction and easily guesse of these things
items.note: The work is addressed to experts who can grasp it at a glance: meant for some readers.

items.quote: who have nothing to doe with the common rabble of Alchymists
items.note: The Sons of Art are set apart from the common rabble of Alchymists.

items.quote: The errors of the Artists are imputed to the Art
items.note: The reproach he reports: artists' errors blamed on the Art; the reason given for the Sons of Art keeping apart from the rabble.

items.quote: He that misseth his end for want of wit, let him thank his own ignorance, & not lay the fault on Nature, or me
items.note: Margin note: failure is the worker's ignorance, not nature's or the author's fault.

items.quote: other operations also which have been proved by the long practice and certain experiments of most expert Chymists and now published in one work
items.note: Some operations published rest on the trials of other expert chymists, not only his own.

items.quote: the true and more profound Phisitians, who have been Divinely inspired
items.note: Names the physicians he means to use these medicines.

items.quote: who in the fear of God also shall use these Medicines rightly prepared by their own labour
items.note: Physicians should prepare the medicines themselves.

items.quote: not trusting (unlesse they would be succeslesse) as many doe, to the Sophistical and fraudulent preparations of others
items.note: Warns against preparations made by others.

items.quote: they will know by experience far greater efficacies and operations by the cures they doe, then I can or ought to set down and assign
items.note: He says there is more than he can or ought to set down: a limit on what is written, resting on the word ought.

items.quote: especially if they be administred according to the nature of the diseased, and with the approbation of a Phisitian present
items.note: How the medicines are to be given: suited to the patient, approved by a physician present.

items.quote: I shall oppose all with the buckler of my sincerity and earnest endeavour of deserving well
items.note: Figure: his sincerity as a shield against critics.

items.quote: the fore-seen darts of the adversary, to wit, anger, evill speaking, envie, scornfull contempt, the truest testimony of ignorance
items.note: The text itself says what the darts are: anger, evil speaking, envy, contempt.

items.quote: Ignorance is the inseparable companion of pride and mischief
items.note: Margin note on the critics' ignorance.

items.quote: The Mysticall Hermetick Philosophers who heretofore in part have pryed into these excellent secrets, will rise against me
items.note: Numbered 1: the first group of opponents he expects.

items.name: Mysticall Hermetick Philosophers
items.quote: which with greatest industry and long spent time have been found out and hitherto concealed in deep silence
items.note: Their expected complaint: what they found and kept hidden in silence is being made common.

items.quote: They will accuse me for breaking open the seale of Chymistry
items.note: Chymistry is said to be sealed; publishing is called breaking the seal.

items.name: Hippocrates
items.quote: To impart sacred things to sacred persons
items.note: Rule given to Hippocrates, which the opponents say he forgot.

items.quote: brought the truth of Chymistry, till this time held captive in the prison of shadowes and envy, freely communicating it to posterity
items.note: The truth of Chymistry is said to have been held captive in shadows until now; he claims to free it.

items.quote: these are the heires of true wisedome, Citizens of the Philosophicall Kingdome, alwayes lovers of God and their neighbor, without envy, or at least ought so to be
items.note: He answers the Hermetick Philosophers that, as heirs of wisdom, they should be without envy.

items.quote: in the true Cabala, Magick and Woarchadumie, there are laid up far better Treasures
items.note: Better treasures are said to be laid up in Cabala, Magick and Woarchadumie: what he publishes is less than what is stored there.

items.quote: A word I doe not understand
items.note: Margin note beside the sentence naming Woarchadumie says a word is not understood; the lines do not show which word or whose voice this is, as it sits oddly with the author's own text (UNCLEAR).

items.quote: with the help of the Oratory and Laboratory, I mean by asking, seeking, and knocking with unwearied paines and watchfullnesse
items.note: The text glosses Oratory and Laboratory as asking, seeking and knocking with unwearied pains.

items.quote: which Treasures are to be manifest indifferently to all in due time by the light of Grace and Nature
items.note: The treasures will be made open to all at a future time.

items.quote: after the Bloody Judgement of the Son is first finished, which undoubtedly will follow the Watry (Judgement) of the Father, then in the third Age of the Holy Spirit
items.what: the third Age of the Holy Spirit
items.note: The text sets out three ages: the Watry Judgement of the Father, the Bloody Judgement of the Son, the third Age of the Holy Spirit.

items.quote: who to make that manifest which was hid, is wont to renew by fire
items.note: The Holy Spirit is said to make the hidden manifest, renewing by fire.

items.quote: Elias the Artist
items.what: Elias the Artist, who is to restore all things
items.note: A figure named as coming in the third age to restore all things.

items.name: Eccl. 43.33.
items.quote: Eccl. 43.33
items.note: Margin note naming a scripture place beside the treasures made manifest by Grace and Nature.

items.name: Zeph. 3.9. Mal. 4.5, 6. Zech 14.9. Ecclesiasticus 48.1,
items.quote: Zeph. 3.9. Mal. 4.5, 6. Zech 14.9. Ecclesiasticus 48.1
items.note: Margin note naming scripture places beside Elias the Artist.

items.quote: For every person of the Divinity hath his own proper and appointed Age, ministry or dispensation
items.note: Each person of the Trinity has his own age.

items.name: Apostles Creed
items.quote: the twelve Articles of the Apostles Creed, divided into three parts
items.note: The Creed's three parts are given as the ground for the three ages.

items.quote: the great and One Day, viz. The continuance of this world
items.note: The text glosses the great and One Day as the continuance of this world; its three hours answer to the three ages.

items.quote: they wil not with me begrudge these present crums to our thankfull posterity
items.note: What he publishes is called crumbs: small set against the better treasures.

items.quote: these Chymicall secrets will never be finger'd by those sluggish, slothfull, or sottish despisers of them
items.note: The secrets protect themselves: the unfit cannot handle them.

items.quote: there will be little danger of their apprehending and discerning these Divine revealed Mysteries, which are mingled together in a fit place
items.note: The mysteries are said to be mingled together in a fit place, so that the profane will not discern them: the text says its contents are arranged to be missed by unworthy readers.

items.quote: which the wise-hearted can apprehend in few words
items.note: The wise-hearted grasp these things from few words: brevity meant for some readers.

items.quote: Only they that are worthy shall understand these things
items.note: Margin note: only the worthy will understand.

items.quote: They whose humane reason God hath inlightned by the mind
items.note: The note says who the worthy are: those whose reason God has enlightened by the mind.

items.quote: Only they that are worthy shall understand these things
items.note: OPEN.2 grounds publication on God giving his light to good and bad alike; here understanding is kept to the worthy. OPEN.2 speaks of God's light, this of these things.

items.quote: As for the spurious and adulterous Theophrasteans (the worst and wickedest sort of men)
items.note: Numbered 2: the second group of opponents.

items.quote: being not able to indure that hereafter they may not carry their cheating impostures up and downe the Country
items.note: The Theophrasteans oppose him because publication ends their cheating trade.

items.quote: snatch up some sentences from the society and conference of other men afterward hunt after a name of learning, wisedome, and prudence among great men, concealing their Authors
items.note: The impostors hide where their knowledge came from; set against N006 on acknowledging sources.

items.quote: sel their forged Cachochymicall and Sophisticall Arts, which have not so much as a spark of truth in them
items.note: False arts are named and set apart from true chymistry.

items.quote: their Pharisaicall skin which hideth the Fox-like and cursed mind would be pluckt off
items.note: Figure: an outward skin hiding the true mind, to be stripped by publication.

items.quote: These seek the commendation of ingenuity from the theft and calumny of their benefactors
items.note: Margin note: the impostors win praise by stealing from and slandering their benefactors.

items.quote: it is truly praise-worthy to displease and vex these Cheaters that are for ever banished the society of all true Philosophers
items.note: Offending the cheaters is praiseworthy; they are outside the true Philosophers.

items.quote: the most laudable and honourable name of true and noble Alchymistry, hath been unworthily made infamous and odious
items.note: True and noble Alchymistry is named as distinct from what the cheaters practise.

items.quote: These are not the vices of the Art, but of men abusing the Art
items.note: Margin note: the faults belong to men, not the Art; agrees with OPEN.7.

items.quote: that Spagyricall or Divinely-distinguishing Sanctuary
items.note: The text glosses Spagyricall as Divinely-distinguishing; compare OPEN.7, Spagyriks as those who discern true from false.

items.quote: what can make a man more renowned then to be dispraised of those most wretched Juglers and effeminate Yonkers
items.note: Blame from such men is called an honour.
